shortDescription: EQS-Media / 16.11.2026 / 09:13 CET/CEST Press release AI-assisted deception in job applications: four in ten recruiters have detected or suspect its use Düsseldorf, November 16, 2026 – Four in ten recruiters (41%) in Germany have identified or suspected cases of AI-assisted deception in recruitment…

children: AI-assisted deception in job applications: four in ten recruiters have detected or suspect its use
New Stepstone survey: 13% of recruiters have identified AI-assisted deception in job applications, while a further 28% suspect it has occurred.
Recruiters report AI-generated answers during job interviews, fabricated references and even impostors attending interviews.
One in six candidates have used AI to exaggerate their skills in job applications. 73% of recruiters have become more sceptical when reviewing jobs applications.

Four in ten recruiters (41%) in Germany have identified or suspected cases of AI-assisted deception in recruitment over the past twelve months. While 13% report confirmed cases, a further 28% suspect such activity. Examples include fabricated references, AI-generated answers during job interviews, and hidden instructions embedded in application documents. These findings come from the latest Hiring Trends Update by The Stepstone Group, which surveyed 7,652 candidates and 1,227 recruiters in Germany. Meanwhile, 73% of recruiters say they have become more sceptical when assessing job applications as AI use among candidates has become increasingly widespread. “Artificial intelligence can do more than just optimise job applications. It creates new opportunities to misrepresent qualifications or deliberately manipulate recruitment processes. And we are only beginning to see its impact. AI will fundamentally change how companies assess applications and verify whether candidates are genuinely suited to a role,” says Dr Christina Langer, Senior Economist at The Stepstone Group. From Fabricated References to Impostors in Job Interviews The survey reveals the various forms of AI-assisted deception recruiters have encountered. Among recruiters who report confirmed cases, 55% have identified exaggerated claims on CVs, 43% fabricated references, and 33% AI-generated answers during live job interviews. Recruiters also report more technically sophisticated attempts at manipulation: 26% have encountered hidden instructions embedded in application documents, known as prompt injections, designed to influence automated selection processes. More strikingly, over one in five (22%) report cases where someone other than the applicant attended the interview. A further 8% have even encountered deepfakes in video interviews. Recruiters also report suspected cases of AI-assisted deception that they could not confirm. The most common involve exaggerated claims on CVs (71%), followed by AI-generated answers during job interviews (30%) and fabricated references (23%). Candidates Admit to Using AI to Exaggerate Their Skills Around half of candidates use AI when applying for jobs, with one in six admitting to using it to exaggerate their skills or experience. Despite this, many candidates still favour human decision-making: 59% prefer a recruitment process without AI, while 61% would not apply for a job if AI made the final hiring decision. “Many candidates believe they need to have the perfect answer to every question in a job interview. AI may seem like a way to achieve that. But a personal interview isn't about delivering rehearsed, textbook answers. It's about getting to know the person behind the application. An honest answer, even if it's not perfectly phrased, often reveals more about someone's actual abilities and personality than a polished, generic AI-generated response,” says Langer. About the Study For the Autumn 2026 Hiring Trends Update, The Stepstone Group surveyed a total of 7,652 candidates and 1,227 recruiters in Germany between 24 September and 13 October 2026. The candidate survey is representative of Germany's working population in terms of age, gender and education (weighted data). The recruiter data is unweighted. The findings on individual forms of deception are based on responses from 505 recruiters who had identified or suspected AI-assisted attempts at deception within the previous twelve months.

Dr Christina Langer is Senior Economist at The Stepstone Group, an economist and labour market researcher focusing on the future of work, generative AI and skills development. Alongside her role at Stepstone, she is an Economist at the ifo Institute and a Digital Fellow at the Stanford Digital Economy Lab, part of the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI. Previously, she conducted research there as a Postdoctoral Researcher on the impact of artificial intelligence, new technologies and changing skill requirements on the labour market, companies and employees. Her work has been published internationally and has been featured by outlets including The New York Times. Throughout her media appearances, discussions and presentations, she combines scientific evidence with practical recommendations for companies, policymakers and the wider public.

The Stepstone Group is a leading global digital recruitment platform that connects companies with the right talent and helps people find the right job. AI-driven job marketplaces and programmatic-powered marketing solutionsconnect more than 130 million job applications with about 70,000 customers every year. The Stepstone Group operates in more than 10 countries - including Stepstone in Germany, Appcast in the USA and Totaljobs in the UK. The company is headquartered in Düsseldorf, Germany and employs more than 2,500 people worldwide. For more information:
